summary: For ages 9–11: polar regions belong to the polar climate zone (one of five main zones: tropical, arid, temperate, continental, polar). Teach latitude — through the angle/spread of sunlight — as the master control that bands the globe from the hot Equator to the cold poles, confront the polar-desert paradox (desert means low precipitation, not heat), and separate weather (day-to-day) from climate (long-term average). Activities move from an interactive latitude-to-climate model through a data-card globe and a climatologist conversation to an answer-plus-reason check.
misconceptions: Deserts are always hot and sandy — polar regions are cold deserts defined by very low precipitation
The poles are snowy so they get lots of precipitation — they receive very little; existing snow just doesn't melt
Climate zones are random bands — they follow latitude because sunlight strikes at different angles
Weather and climate are the same — climate is the long-term average pattern, not today's conditions
It's cold at the poles mainly because they are far from the Sun — it's the low ANGLE/spread of sunlight with latitude, not distance

activities.title: Drag latitude from Equator to pole and watch the climate zone change
steps: Drag a marker up the face of a globe from the Equator toward the pole and observe what happens as latitude rises.
Watch an inset showing the Sun's rays change from striking straight-down and concentrated (at the Equator) to slanting in and spreading thin across the surface (near the pole).

Read a falling thermometer and the zone label changing (for example tropical → temperate → polar in this simplified model) as the marker climbs; in the real world, the arid and continental zones also depend on other factors, such as distance from the sea.
At the South Pole (Antarctic interior), open a data card comparing its average yearly precipitation with the Sahara's average and notice the polar value is LOWER.
Toggle a weather/climate control to contrast one stormy day with a decades-long average for the same place.
activities.insight: Latitude, through the angle and spread of sunlight, is what carves Earth into climate zones; the icy pole is a cold desert because 'desert' is about how little precipitation falls, not how hot it is.

activities.title: Explore a banded climate-zone globe with data cards
steps: Tap each band of a globe shaded from tropical Equator to polar caps and read its latitude label.
Open climate-zone data cards showing temperature and precipitation for each zone, including the polar-desert figure alongside the Sahara.
Sort or match several named places (e.g. a tropical rainforest, a hot desert, the Antarctic interior) to the correct climate zone using the cards.
activities.insight: Climate zones broadly follow latitude in bands (other factors, such as distance from the sea, also shape the arid and continental zones), and the very low precipitation of the polar interior makes it a desert despite its ice and cold.

activities.title: Talk it through with a climatologist
steps: Ask and answer questions about why climate zones band the globe and why the poles are cold.
Explain in your own words why the Sahara and central Antarctica are both deserts yet feel completely different.
Respond to the question: 'What if lots of snow suddenly started falling on Antarctica every day — would it still be a desert?'
activities.insight: Articulating the latitude–sunlight–climate chain and the precipitation definition of a desert in dialogue consolidates the reasoning and surfaces lingering confusions.

activities.title: How can freezing, icy Antarctica be a desert?
steps: Read: 'A geographer says the middle of Antarctica is one of the biggest DESERTS on Earth, yet it is covered in ice and freezing cold.' Decide whether it can be a desert.
Give your answer, then give the REASON why it counts (or doesn't).
Answer a follow-up: 'So what actually makes somewhere a desert — give the rule in your own words.'
activities.insight: A desert is defined by very low precipitation, not by heat; Antarctica's interior qualifies because scant snow falls and almost never melts, building up over a very long time.

checkQuestion: A geographer says the middle of Antarctica is one of the biggest DESERTS on Earth. But Antarctica is covered in ice and it's freezing cold — how can a place that cold and icy be called a desert? Tell me, and then tell me WHY it counts as a desert.
checkAnswer: A desert is defined by how little PRECIPITATION it gets, not by heat. The interior of Antarctica gets extremely little snow or rain — less than the Sahara — so it qualifies as a desert (a cold or polar desert). The ice is there because it is so cold that the tiny amount of snow that does fall almost never melts and has built up over a very long time, not because it snows a lot.
